name: Helios-Nomad Stormline Shell
description:
A minimalist hardshell rain jacket from Helios-Nomad, a mid-tier outdoor brand that pivoted hard into urban commuter wear in the 2180s. The shell is a three-layer bonded membrane — waterproof, windproof, breathable — in a clean matte finish. No visible seams on the outside; all taped internally. The cut is slim without being restrictive. Hood stows flat into the collar. Two hand pockets and a chest pocket, all waterproof-zip. Available in a range of solid colors: slate, sand, a particular deep teal that's become associated with the brand.

This is the jacket you wear in GLMZ's persistent lake-effect weather — the cold drizzle that runs October through April, the sudden squalls off Lake Michigan that soak you in ninety seconds. It's practical and it looks it. Tier 2 commuters wear it because it works. Tier 3 buyers wear it because it also happens to look clean. It photographs well. It layers over everything. It's the closest thing to a universal jacket the city has.
what_it_says: You've thought about the weather and made a decision. Practical but not careless. The teal colorway suggests you also thought about the color.
worn_by: anyone who walks to work in a lake city
story_hooks: Helios-Nomad's teal colorway was originally a limited run for a city transit worker uniform contract that fell through — the surplus stock hit retail and sold out in a week, creating a color association the brand now leans into deliberately.

A Shelf-based counterfeit operation has been selling fake Stormline Shells with a shell that looks identical but fails within two weeks of rain exposure — and the fakes have a slightly different teal shade that requires side-by-side comparison to spot.

A Tier 3 urban planner who wears one of these every day has started marking jacket pockets with small adhesive dots — a personal notation system for tracking which pocket holds which item in the dark. Someone is using the same system for entirely different reasons.
